PROJECT DESCRIPTION
2.1 Purposes and Project Objectives
2.1.1.1 The Project’s objective is to deliver a new road connecting Yuen Long Highway/
Tsing Long Highway and Fanling Highway, linking key new development nodes
such as Ngau Tam Mei New Development Area (NTM NDA) and San Tin
Technopole (STT).
2.2 Location, Site History, and Scope of the Project
2.2.1.1 The location of the Project is shown in Figure 1.1.
2.2.1.2 The alignment of the Project (San Tin Section) starts at the interchange of Yuen
Long Highway / Tsing Long Highway on the west, and traverses the developed area
in Mo Fan Heung, which are presently brownfield sites. It passes through the
conservation areas near Fung Kat Heung and Ngau Tam Mei, goes underground
at Ngau Tam Shan. The alignment travels along the villages near Saddle Pass,
extends through the conservation areas near San Tin, continues underground at
Hadden Hill (Ki Lun Shan), and finally connects to the Fanling Highway (Pak Shek
Au Section).
2.2.1.3 Historically, the project site was predominantly rural and occupied by agricultural
activities and village settlements. Currently, low-density residential development at
Mo Fan Heung, Pok Wai, Kwu Tung, etc., villages such as Yau Tam Mei Tsuen, Ki
Lun Tsuen, scattered brownfield operations, farmland/fishponds are found within or
in the vicinity of the project.
2.2.1.4 The scope of the Project is to provide a carriageway connecting Yuen Long
Highway/ Tsing Long Highway and Fanling Highway (Pak Shek Au Section). It
comprises the following key elements, the general layout is shown in Figure 2.1.
(a) Construction of an approximately 9.0-kilometre (km) long dual three-lane
carriageway, mainly in the form of at-grade road / tunnel / viaduct. In total,
about 2.5 km is in the form of tunnel in mainline;
(b) Construction of five interchanges located at Yuen Long Highway/Tsing Long
Highway, Ngau Tam Mei NDA, San Tin Technopole, Fanling Highway and
Kwu Tung North NDA. This includes approximately 150m tunnel length at the
interchange slip road connecting STT; and
(c) Associated junction modifications and slip roads required for the project, civil,
geotechnical, landscape, road and drainage works, ancillary buildings, traffic
control and surveillance system, toll collection facilities, electrical and
mechanical installations, reprovisioning of facilities affected by the proposed
works, environmental mitigation measures and administration building / kiosk,
portal plant building/ plant room, etc.

2.3 Need for the Project
2.3.1.1 With the progressive development of STT and NTM NDA, traffic congestion is
anticipated at San Tin Highway during peak hours in 2036. The Project will alleviate
the San Tin Highway traffic congestion by providing an alternative route.
2.3.1.2 In longer term, the transport demand for east-west connectivity within the Northern
Metropolis and cross-boundary connections is projected to increase substantially –
driven by the progressive development of the Northern Metropolis and the gradual
increase on the residential and employment population. The Project, together with
the other three sections of NMH, can provide alternative route from New Territories
East and West, and alleviate the traffic congestion on Yuen Long Highway, San Tin
Highway and Fanling Highway.
2.4 Benefits and Alternative Mitigation Measures of the Project
2.4.1.1 The Project can bring the following benefits:
Environmental Benefits and Environmentally Friendly Design
(a) Avoidance of direct impact to ecologically sensitive areas - The recommended
alignment and its works footprint have been thoroughly considered and
evaluated from alternative alignment options proposed in previous stage
studies (Section 2.6 refers). This process has resulted in the recommended
alignment option, which aims to avoid both the direct and indirect potential
impacts on recognised sites of conservation importance and other ecologically
sensitive areas, such as the Lam Tsuen Country Park (LTCP), the proposed
Nam Sang Wai Wetland Conservation Park and natural watercourses at Ngau
Tam Mei. The locations of piers are also carefully designed to be outside the
Ngau Tam Mei natural watercourses.
(b) Wetland Habitat Enhancement through Integration and Expansion – Under the
original alignment, an interchange, I/C-03, (with associated site office and
ancillary facilities) was proposed to the west of Ngau Tam Mei Water
Treatment Works (NTMWTW), where scattered and fragmented wetland
habitats are currently found. Compared to the original alignment, the
recommended alignment has been refined, with the Interchange I/C-03
relocated to the south of NTM NDA (refer to Figure 2.1.2). The viaduct level
has also been raised as much as practicable to provide greater clearance
allowing natural sunlight to reach the habitats underneath the viaduct
structures. The relocation of Interchange I/C-03 to the south of NTM NDA will
also provide an opportunity to integrate and expand the wetland habitats to the
west of NTMWTW (refer to Figure 2.1.3). Furthermore, the mainline will be
constructed as an elevated viaduct with a limited number of piers, spanning
over the wetland habitats to reduce direct ecological impact to this wetland
habitats. Taking advantage of the Project implementation, the area will not only
be reinstated, but the existing fragmented wetland habitats will also be
integrated and enhanced into a connected wetland habitat. The total wetland
area will increase from approximately 3 hectares of fragmented ponds to more
than 5 hectares of integrated wetland habitats through the incorporation of
adjacent village / orchard land. With improved design and management, the

(c) Allowing Wildlife Movement by Adopting Intermittent At‑grade and Viaduct
Design – A section of the alignment runs adjacent to the woodland habitat at

profile has been raised as far as practicable, taking into account site
constraints such as CLP cables, pylons and traffic design requirements. The

The space beneath the viaduct sections provides an open corridor to facilitate
wildlife movement to and from LTCP. For the at-grade sections, retaining wall
on the slope would be constructed to avoid wildlife roadkill.
(d) Viaduct Level Arrangement and Carriageway Separation for Enhancing
Sunlight Penetration and Ecological Benefits – The Project includes slip roads
crossing the Kam Tin River (refer to Figure 2.1.1), where the viaduct level has
been adjusted to provide headroom of about 10~15m and minimise shading
effects on the water body and associated habitats. In the vicinity of NTMWTW,
to accommodate the required clearance from the existing CLP cable, the
headroom beneath the viaduct is approximately 10m for the northbound and
ranges from 5m to 10m for the southbound. The dual carriageways are
separated before entering the tunnel portal (refer to Figure 2.1.3). The
resulting gap between the carriageways enables natural sunlight to reach the
ground below and is not expected to cause adverse ecological impacts.
Furthermore, the positioning of piers have been refined to avoid encroachment
into natural watercourses. This approach helps to minimize potential water
quality and ecological impact.
(e) Adoption of Non-dredged Method for Construction Works at Kam Tin River -
The significance of ecological value of Kam Tin River is well recognised. Given
the large span of the viaduct crossing Kam Tin River, the pile /pier support
within the river is inevitable (refer to Figure 2.1.1). The construction of viaduct
pier/ pile will adopt the non-dredging method. For example, if bored pile
construction is adopted, steel casing could be adopted to isolate the
surrounding riverbed. The material within the steel casing will be excavated
within the casing for placing reinforcement and concrete of the pile. This
minimises the disturbance to the river.
(f) Synergistic Woodland Enhancement near She Leng – A Woodland
compensation of approximately 17 ha is proposed near She Leng, which is
currently characterised by grassland or shrubland of low or low to moderate
ecological value. The site is also adjacent to proposed woodland compensation
areas under other projects, including Lok Ma Chau Loop, STT and
Development of the Loop – Eastern Connection Road (ECR). Woodland
compensation at this location will integrate the overall compensatory woodland
area and improve habitat quality and ecological connectivity with adjacent
woodland habitats.

retaining walls / soil nails or combination of both may be proposed. This

gradients, and thereby minimise the project’s environmental footprint, as well
as acting as a barrier to prevent wildlife roadkill.

any excavation works which will cause potential disturbance to the soil matrix
within the boundary of Ngau Tam Mei SAI to avoid potential direct impacts on
the SAI (refer to Figure 2.1.2).

method over TBM (Tunnel Boring Machine) method for tunnel construction to
minimize the generation of C&D materials as much as practicable.

Territories, lowering vehicular emissions from idling or congested traffic and
shortening travel times and results in further reducing fuel consumption,

Scenario “without” Project
2.5.2.1 Without the implementation of the Project, traffic congestion would be expected at
road section of San Tin Highway in year 2036 during peak hour with the progressive
development of development nodes such as STT and the NTM NDA.
2.5.2.2 The connectivity of development nodes will not be as direct and convenient as with
the Project which in turn limits the potential of development area.
2.5.2.3 The overstress of existing road network would cause traffic congestion which in turn
induces potential air quality and noise impacts to the sensitive receivers.
2.5.2.4 Without the Project, the east-west traffic connection in Northern Metropolis would
heavily rely on the existing San Tin Highway which will operate beyond its capacity.
2.6 Consideration of Alignment Options
General
2.6.1.1 The alignment under the Project consists of 5 interchanges (I/C-02 to I/C-06) from
Yuen Long Highway / Tsing Long Highway to Fanling Highway. Interim
interchanges (I/C-03 to I/C-05) are provided to connect some development nodes
and existing roads. The I/C-02 and I/C-06 will reserve stub ends for connection to
the future Tin Shui Wai section and Kwu Tung section of NMH respectively.
(a) I/C-02 will reserve stub end at west for future connection to Tin Shui Wai
Section of NMH.
(b) I/C-02 to I/C-03 connects Yuen Long Highway/ Tsing Long Highway and NTM
NDA
(c) I/C-03 to I/C-04 connects NTM NDA and STT
(d) I/C-04 to I/C-05 connects STT and Fanling Highway
(e) I/C-05 to I/C-06 connects Fanling Highway and Kwu Tung North NDA
(f) I/C-06 will reserve stub end at north for future connection to Kwu Tung Section
of NMH
2.6.1.2 Original Alignment Option was initially derived from the SSMR FS under Agreement
No. CE7/2018(TT).
2.6.1.3 After commencement of the Investigation stage, more detailed analysis has been
conducted, and several alignment options have been further explored aiming to
optimise the scheme and to enhance environmental benefits.
2.6.1.4 With preliminary review and screening, three alignment options (inclusive of the
Original Alignment Option) have been shortlisted and taken forward for evaluation
from perspectives of site constraints, traffic performance, engineering
constructability, social acceptance, environmentally friendliness, etc to suggest the
recommended alignment.

2.6.1.5 Alignment Option 3 is recommended after robust considerations. Figure 2.2
(Figure 2.2.1-2.2.4) delineates the three alignment options. Sections below present
the considerations of alignment options with elaboration.
Alignment Option 1 (Original Alignment)
2.6.2.1 The original alignment is primarily designed as an underground scheme to avoid
encroachment upon above-ground constraints.
I/C-02 to I/C-03
2.6.2.2 The mainline of alignment would be constructed in the form of tunnel from Nam
Sang Wai Wetland and across the Kam Tin River from future Tin Shui Wai Section
of NMH at west (refer to Figure 2.2.1). In view of the geological condition, Tunnel
Boring Machine (TBM) tunnels, supported by a shaft each at two ends for the
launching and retrieving TBM, is proposed for the underground section at the west
of LTCP before entering the hill. Both shafts will be constructed using the open cut
method—this involves digging deep, large-scale excavation and installing lateral
support structures to keep the excavation stable. After entering the LTCP where the
terrain is hilly, tunnelling will be carried out primarily using the drill-and-blast method,
with localised supplementary mechanical breaking where necessary.
2.6.2.3 To provide the connection at I/C-02 to existing San Tin Highway while catering the
level difference, depressed slip roads are required to connect the existing at-grade
San Tin Highway near Mo Fang Heung and tunnel mainline. The alignment mainline
keeps the tunnel form and traverses the LTCP in parallel to existing water tunnel at
south. The mainline tunnel would go under the existing Ngau Tam Mei Water
Reservoir and the existing underground Express Rail Link (XRL) (refer to Figure
2.2.2).
2.6.2.4 Before arriving at the existing NTMWTW, the alignment curves towards north and
become day light section given the topographical feature. The mainline and I/C-03
would be accommodated between the narrow strip of land between the existing
NTMWTW and the future NTM NDA (refer to Figure 2.2.3).
I/C-03 to I/C-04
2.6.2.5 After I/C-03 and the NTMWTW, the alignment curves toward east to across the
Ngau Tam Shan in tunnel form (refer to Figure 2.2.3) and then bends north
subsequently toward the next connection I/C-04 which would become day light
section connecting the STT. The I/C-04 location is considerately selected at the low
point between Ngau Tam Shan and Hadden Hill (refer to Figure 2.2.4) to minimise
the site formation while not encroaching the STT. This inevitably creates a double
curve tunnel layout between I/C-03 and I/C-04.
I/C-04 to I/C-05
2.6.2.6 After the I/C-04, the alignment encounters the Hadden Hill and changes to tunnel
form in parallel to the existing water tunnel. At the west side of existing Kwu Tung
Reservoir, there is small section of valley which requires the alignment to span
over in viaduct form. After passing the Hadden Hill, the alignment becomes day
light section at I/C-05 to provide connection to Fanling Highway in viaduct form
(refer to Figure 2.2.4).

Construction of Tunnels
2.7.5.1 Based on the available geological profile, it is envisaged that tunnel excavation will
be mostly carried out in good quality volcanic rock masses. They are typically
excavated by drill & blast (D&B) method. Other forms of excavation such as
mechanical and chemical splitting are not cost effective except for either small
volume of excavation or at locations where blasting would pose too great nuisance
or be hazard (e.g. in close proximity to sensitive receivers). When encountering
softground (e.g. soil layer) or low cover conditions, mechanical excavation with
robust temporary support would be adopted.
2.7.5.2 TBM has been assessed and considered inappropriate for adoption for the Project,
based on the considerations set out below.
• The largest hard‑rock TBM available globally is approximately 15 m in diameter,
which is below 16m to 19m span required for 3-lane tunnels with sightline
widening in the Project.
• TBM involves relatively high initial capital investment and longer mobilisation
periods, particularly associated with the setting of launching and receiving areas
and machine mobilisation.
• TBMs inherently create circular cross‑sections in fixed dimensions, which does
not match with the flat inverts and variable internal geometry (e.g. sightline
widening) required for the Project. Using a TBM would therefore result in
significant over‑excavation and C&D materials.
• Large‑diameter TBM typically achieves low production rates of around 2m/day
in hard rock stratum. By comparison, D&B performs very efficiently in hard rock
and can achieve advance rates of larger than 5m per blast under favourable
conditions.
2.7.5.3 D&B method is a cyclic operation comprising activities of drilling - blasting –
mucking – installing support.
2.7.5.4 The supply of explosives for blasting relies on a daily delivery from Mines Division.
This delivery is typically made between 11am and 2pm each day, and the
explosives are expected to be used immediately, limiting to a single blast each day
during the afternoon. In order to expedite the tunnel excavation with minimised idle
time in the blast cycle and mitigate the potential risk of missing out the explosives
delivery by Mines Division due to unforeseen site conditions e.g. extra time for
temporary support, machine malfunction, an explosive magazine is required to
allow flexible blasting time.
2.7.5.5 During blasting operations, the blast door at the tunnel portal will be closed to
contain blasting activities within the tunnel and separate them from the surrounding
environment, thereby effectively controlling potential air quality and noise impacts.
